# IELTS Speaking Part 2 - Model Answers (Band 7-8)

---

## Model Answer 1: A Place You Go to Relax

**Describe a place you go to when you want to relax.**

I'd like to talk about a small park called Cubbon Park, which is right in the centre of Bangalore, only about a fifteen-minute walk from my office. It's not particularly large by city-park standards, but it has these enormous old rain trees whose canopies meet over the paths, and the whole place feels several degrees cooler than the streets around it.

I try to go two or three times a week, usually after work when the light is starting to soften. My routine is fairly simple: I do one slow loop of about twenty-five minutes, then I sit on the same bench near the bandstand and either read for a bit or call my mum, who lives in another city and likes to hear about my day. Sometimes I just sit and watch other people doing the same thing, which is oddly companionable.

The reason it helps me relax is partly physical and partly mental. Physically, just being under that much greenery seems to slow me down — my breathing changes, I notice I'm not gripping my phone so tightly. Mentally, it's the one part of the day where I deliberately leave notifications switched off, so no one can interrupt me with a Slack message or a calendar reminder. After about half an hour I usually walk home feeling that whatever was bothering me at three o'clock has lost most of its weight.

## Model Answer 2: A Teacher Who Influenced You

**Describe a teacher who has influenced you.**

I'd like to describe my year-eleven physics teacher, Mr Holloway, who I still remember vividly more than ten years after leaving school. He had been an aerospace engineer before retraining as a teacher, which gave him a slightly different angle on the subject from teachers who'd come straight out of university.

He taught us standard GCSE physics, but what made his classes different was his refusal to start with the equations. When we were studying projectile motion, for example, he wheeled in a small model trebuchet that he'd built at home, fired it across the lab, and asked us to predict where the ball would land. We were almost always wrong on the first try, and only then did he write the formulas on the board, this time with our wrong predictions sitting next to them as motivation.

What also made him different was that he took mistakes seriously. Instead of just saying 'no, that's wrong', he would ask 'walk me through how you got there', and the whole class would learn from somebody else's reasoning.

The influence has lasted in two ways. First, I went on to study mechanical engineering at university partly because of him — I genuinely came to enjoy the kind of problem he set us. Second, even now in my work, I try to ask 'walk me through your reasoning' whenever someone disagrees with me. That single phrase came from him and it has saved me from a lot of unnecessary arguments.

## Model Answer 3: A Gift You Received

**Describe a gift you received that meant a lot to you.**

I'd like to describe a leather notebook that my older sister gave me the night before I left home for university. She had bought it during a study-abroad year in Florence, which meant she'd been carrying it around in her suitcase for months waiting for the right moment to hand it over.

It's a dark-tan A5 notebook with a soft leather cover and stitched binding. The paper is unusually thick, so ink doesn't bleed through to the next page, which I noticed straight away. Tucked inside the front cover, she'd written a paragraph wishing me luck and listing three things she hoped I'd remember to do during my degree.

I received it on a slightly emotional evening — we hadn't lived in the same city for nearly two years and we both knew that pattern was unlikely to change once I started university.

The reason it meant so much wasn't really the object, although I genuinely love the feel of it. It was the fact that she'd already written in it. That single page made it impossible to keep it on a shelf as a museum piece; I had to use it. I now use it as a journal and I'm probably halfway through. I'll be sad when it runs out, but I think the next one will feel slightly easier to start because of this one.

## Model Answer 4: A Memorable Journey

**Describe a memorable journey you have taken.**

I'd like to talk about an overnight train journey I took from Bangalore to Goa with my best friend Priya about three years ago. We were both finishing university and had decided to take a short trip before we started job-hunting properly.

The train was supposed to leave at nine in the evening and arrive in Goa around eight the next morning. In the end, it left almost six hours late because of an issue further up the line, and we ended up sitting on the platform for most of the night with a couple of other equally annoyed passengers.

What made it memorable, though, wasn't the holiday in Goa, which was perfectly nice but slightly forgettable. It was that night on the platform. Once we'd accepted that the train wasn't coming any time soon, the four of us shared whatever snacks we had in our bags, swapped stories, and ended up watching the sunrise together over the railway tracks. By the time the train finally arrived, the actual journey almost felt like an anticlimax.

The reason it has stayed with me is that it taught me something I didn't really understand at the time: small disasters on a trip are often what you remember most clearly. The beach photos all look the same after a few years, but that strange, oddly companionable night on a half-empty platform is the part of the holiday I can still describe in detail.

## Model Answer 5: A Useful Piece of Technology

**Describe a useful piece of technology you own.**

The piece of technology I'd like to describe is my pair of noise-cancelling headphones. They're not a particularly recent or unusual purchase, but they have probably had a bigger effect on my day-to-day life than any gadget I've bought in the last few years.

I use them almost every day. On weekday mornings I put them on for the walk to the bus stop, which is along a fairly busy road, and again for an hour or two at the office whenever I need to concentrate on something complex. I also use them for calls, particularly during meetings I take from cafés.

What I mainly use them for is focus rather than music. Our office is open-plan, which sounds nice in theory but in practice means there's always somebody on a call or a courier ringing the buzzer. The headphones essentially carve out a small private workspace inside the noise, so I can read a long document or write a careful email without losing my train of thought every two minutes.

The reason I find them so useful is that they've made me far less dependent on having the perfect environment. Five years ago, if my office was noisy, I'd just give up and try again the next day. Now I can effectively work from anywhere — a café, an airport, a friend's living room — which means a surprising amount of what used to feel like wasted time has become productive. They probably pay for themselves several times over each year in that sense.

## Model Answer 6: A Time You Helped Someone

**Describe a time you helped someone.**

I'd like to talk about an evening last winter when I helped an elderly neighbour after she'd fallen on her front step. I was walking home from work and noticed her sitting on the path looking quite shaken. She lives two doors down from me, but we'd only ever exchanged hellos before, so I introduced myself properly before doing anything else.

The situation was that she'd slipped on a small patch of ice and bruised her hip, and although nothing seemed to be broken, she didn't think she could stand without help. I rang the non-emergency NHS line because I genuinely wasn't sure what the right thing to do was, and they advised that we wait for a paramedic just to be safe.

While we waited, which turned out to be almost an hour, I went into her kitchen and made her a cup of tea, fetched a blanket from the sofa, and sat with her on the step. We ended up having a long conversation about her late husband and the changes she'd seen on the street over the past forty years. The paramedic eventually checked her over, helped her inside, and confirmed she was fine.

I felt two things afterwards. The first was a quiet sense of being useful, which is rarer than I'd like in a desk job. The second was slight embarrassment that we'd lived next door for over a year without my ever properly introducing myself. I now stop and chat with her every time I see her, and that's been a small but real change in how my street feels.
